extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the foundations of science
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of the kinds of logical terms and propositions and the governing laws of their combination and inference (e.g., law of contradiction, simplicity, commutativeness, intension/extension relation). Explains how to form symbolic expressions and what counts as valid/invalid combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms denote extent and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is said to denote the object of thought to which it may be applied; it implies at the same time the possession of certain qualities or circumstances. The objects denoted form the extent of meaning of the term; the qualities implied form the intent of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Crystal' — extent = substances whose molecules are regularly arranged; intent = the circumstance of molecular arrangement. Use both aspects when analyzing meanings; distinguish what a term applies to (extent) from the qualities it implies (intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation of intension and extension
rubrics_metrics.description: When the intent of meaning of a term is increased the extent is decreased; and vice versa, when the extent is increased the intent is decreased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a universal logical law for changes of meaning. Example: prefixing 'external' or 'nearest to the earth' to 'planet' increases intension and reduces extension (ultimately to a single object). Adding adjectives increases intension (fewer objects), removing them decreases it (more objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms possess single intension and are incapable of plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract terms are strongly distinguished from general terms by possessing only one kind of meaning; for they denote qualities there is nothing which they cannot inhere in of red objects, but this latter term has one single meaning — the quality alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'redness' denotes the single quality shared by red objects and so is one and the same everywhere. Speaking of 'rednesses' introduces concreteness (different kinds or tints) and so alters meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial terms: unity like abstract terms though concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain terms (substantial terms) partake of the unity of abstract terms though they name concrete substances (e.g., gold, carbonate of lime, nitrogen). We cannot speak of two golds in the sense of different kinds; the substance is one in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial terms denote a uniform substance whose qualities pervade it; plurality arises only when physical division creates distinguishable pieces (e.g., 'piece of gold'). Use this distinction when treating counting/plurality vs. nature of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective versus general terms — do not infer whole from parts or vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the collective and the general meanings of terms. The same name may denote the whole aggregate of existing objects of a kind or any one of those objects separately. One must not infer of a collective whole what is known only of the parts, nor of the parts what is known only of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'man' may mean 'mankind' (aggregate) or any individual man. Beware substitution errors between whole and part (whole ≠ identity with parts), though some qualities may hold alike of whole and parts (e.g., organ-pipes tuned in unison produce sound of same pitch as each).

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of terms by juxtaposition in symbolic language
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase the intension of a term we join adjectives, phrases, or other terms; in symbolic language the juxtaposition of letter-terms indicates this junction (e.g., if A = brittle and B = metal, then AB means 'brittle metal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No limit to the number or complexity of letters joined (example forming PQRSTV to denote a metal with multiple specified properties). Nouns, prepositional phrases, participial phrases, and subordinate propositions may be added logically as adjectives; symbols let us ignore grammatical peculiarities and focus on logical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synbolic neglect of grammatical peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many grammatical usages concerning junction of words and phrases to which logic need pay no attention; in symbols we may treat equivalent phrases and adjectives as logically interchangeable (e.g., 'of wood' ≡ 'wooden').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic letter-terms permit treating phrases as adjectives when convenient (e.g., SP means 'metal of specific gravity 10.5'). The point is to focus on logical relations rather than grammatical form; be cautious where exact grammatical form does matter semantically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Contradiction — self-contradictory combinations excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: No quality can be both present and absent at the same time and place. A term and its negative shall never be allowed to come into combination; such combined terms as Aa, Bb, Cc are self-contradictory and devoid of intelligible meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolise the impossible/self-contradictory by the cipher o: Aa = o, ABa = o, ABCa = o. The criterion of false reasoning is that it involves self-contradiction (affirming and denying the same statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special condition — repetition (Law of Simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of a logical term with itself is without effect: repetition of a term does not alter meaning; 'a round round object' is simply 'a round object'. In symbols A = AA = AAA = &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the Law of Simplicity. It is important when relating logical and mathematical symbols; repetition should be treated as identity rather than multiplicity. Examples and historical notes (Boole, Boethius) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutativeness of simple logical synthesis (order indifferent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order of combination is a matter of indifference in simple logical synthesis: AB is identical with BA, ABC = ACB = BCA = &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property (Commutativeness) applies to simple conjunctions of properties/qualities where order carries no logical significance. Do NOT apply commutativeness to relations involving time, space, or order-sensitive relations (e.g., 'A killing B' ≠ 'B killing A'); the law belongs only to simple logical synthesis, not to relational structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of inference — identity of the like or same
rubrics_metrics.description: All propositions admit the application of the one same principle of inference that what is true of a thing is true of the like or same. This principle holds whatever be the kind or manner of the likeness, provided proper regard be had to its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions can assert identity of time, space, manner, quantity, degree, etc.; when two things are identical in the relevant respect, truths about one transfer to the other (examples: same year of birth/death, same place, equal density). Apply the principle only with attention to the nature of the identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple identities (A = B) as fundamental propositions and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important class of propositions consists of those which fall under the formula A = B, called simple identities. Many elementary propositions state exact similarity of a quality encountered in two or more objects. All definitions are necessarily of this form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Colour of Pacific Ocean = Colour of Atlantic Ocean', 'Common salt = Sodium chloride', 'Equilateral triangles = Equiangular triangles'. Use A = B to express identity of single qualities, groups of qualities, singular identifications, and definitions. Grammatical forms that combine several propositions must be analyzed into such identities.
